A unit is two officers; a robot is an armed patrol unit, and robots count toward the cap of 30 combatants. An alarm sends the response to the scene, then to where the missing person's post, car and closest people are meant to be, then to the people the alarm-raiser knows. Robots only go within 60 m of where they start. Fighting your way out is a last resort, not a route.

Watchers log everyone Spec

Cameras and civic robots stand at key places on the district plan: stations, stops, gates and squares. Anyone in their line of sight is logged with a place and a time, whatever they are doing. Once a Trail is open, investigators can pull the log, and every sighting becomes a lead. If the cell is hot (Heat over its threshold) or its Standing in the district is Menace, a sighting counts as a witness report and raises Alert.

Investigators follow the trail Spec

City management works the streets in real time. Units on foot question someone about every 20 s; cars cover ground fast and stop to question. More come out as Alert and Trail rise. They pick civilians near the last incident by sightline and distance, not by luck. A useful answer is a fact with a place and a time: they go there and question again, closing in lead by lead, roughly 60–90 s per hop.

The player sees it happen: a questioning icon, a dotted line joining the leads they hold, and the unit following it. Counters: keep moving so a sighting goes stale, reach a witness first (pay, reassure or threaten, and threats raise fear), send them the wrong way with the Scout's false tip, block their cars with citizens, or break sightlines in a crowd. What they learn carries into the debrief's Investigation state and the next mission. In a Hero campaign, brave locals feed them false leads.

06 · FIGHTS

The test of how much of the city is yours

Fights are real and grow as you rise. They aren't a separate combat game: they are fast and real-time, like Syndicate, short and lethal, and decided by what you prepared. They measure your preparation: arms bought, contacts brave enough to stand with you, and streets that decide whose side they are on.

How fights escalate Spec

  • How often depends on Heat = campaign Trail + Menace standing. Crossing a Heat threshold schedules a fight event (a raid, an ambush, a rival hit) in the next mission. No dice. The district's security level (§05) is a separate axis: Heat brings fights to the cell, the security level makes a district watch harder.
  • How big depends on the act: 3–6 hostiles in act I, 8–15 in act II, 20–30 in act III. The hard cap is 30 actively simulated combatants. Everyone else is background crowd that can only run or cheer.
  • Your side = cell + Accomplice/Fighter contacts + crowd joiners (Hero standing), armed up to your Arms stock.

What citizens can do

Scatter

Panic that breaks enemy sightlines and covers a retreat.

Block

Park a lorry, stall a tram or fill a street to stop police vehicles.

Join

Fight bare-handed, or armed if you have the Arms.

Vehicle strike

Ram a barricade, or send a rigged vehicle. The driver always jumps clear.

Content line. Civilians are never the payload. A coerced person driving a bomb is a suicide attack, which is a problem for age rating, store listing and press, and a tone the game should not carry. The Menace version can be uglier (collateral damage, witnesses who saw who forced them), but no civilian dies as the weapon.

Syndicate-style fights Spec

The whole cell can be armed. Any operative can carry a sidearm, one per point of Arms; the Enforcer's carbine belongs to the cell and uses none. The Enforcer stays the heavy: the carbine, the most health, and the only one who carries Vale. The Handover issues all four guns; the campaign starts with the Fixer alone and no Arms.

WeaponDamageFires everyPoint blankEffectiveLong
Pistol11.5 sUp to 5 m: every shot hitsUp to 15 m: 3 in 4Up to 25 m: 2 in 5
Carbine22.0 sUp to 5 m: every shot hitsUp to 20 m: 3 in 4Up to 30 m: 2 in 5

Hits halve when the shooter is walking or the target stands still beside cover. The Enforcer holding Vale, and anyone untrained (the Scout, Fixer and Tech, and rivals), hit three quarters as often. There are no reloads or ammunition: Arms is the limit. Drawing takes 1 s, the first shot at a new target 1 s, and a hostile caught by surprise reacts in 2 s.

No dice. A hit is a rate, not a roll: at 3 in 4, exactly three shots in four hit. So the cursor can say "hits 3 in 4 · down in 5.5 s", and every loss is the player's own.

Orders. Fire keeps shooting until the target is down; an operative who walks keeps firing at the walking rate, one who runs stops. Cease fire stops it. There are three stances: hold (fire only when ordered), return (the default: fire back at whoever fires on you) and at will (any combatant in reach, nearest first). Once a fight is on, the panic order sends every armed operative to fire at will. Stances and panic only ever shoot combatants, never a civilian, a contact, Vale, or a guard or patrol that hasn't engaged, so only an explicit order to fire starts a loud run.

Hostiles advance to cover worked out at build time, stop and shoot once in range, and pick first whoever is shooting at them, then whoever holds Vale, then the nearest operative. Rivals break when more than half of them are down; police hold. Crowds within 30 m of gunfire scatter.

Everyone has health, shown as pips when selected and over everyone in a fight. Starting values: civilian 2, guard or officer 3, rival 3, patrol unit 4, Scout, Fixer and Tech 4, Enforcer 6. Weapons bought with Arms set damage and fire rate, from a pistol (1 damage) to heavier guns (2–3). Armour and healing come through people, not upgrades: a quartermaster supplies armour, a turned doctor heals.

Down, not dead. An operative at 0 is downed. Another operative can carry them to the car (lifting takes 3 s; the carrier walks and doesn't fire); if they are left behind, they are captured, and freeing them becomes a mission.

Silent takedowns. "In theory can take out anyone, but it's all about being seen or not … Killing a civilian in front of a camera as a lone gunman is highly likely to end in failure" (Sky). There is no list of who may be targeted; the cost comes only from who sees it. The Enforcer, within arm's reach, knocks a person out (6 s) or kills them (3 s), in silence: no gunfire rule applies. A target who sees him coming struggles (+3 s), screams and remembers his face; an armed one turns it into a fight. Someone knocked out wakes and talks unless hidden, tied up or turned. Someone killed never talks, but a body that is found is far worse (§05, §08). The patrol robot and cameras are not targets (the Tech has its own verbs for them); killing Vale fails the mission, and he can't be knocked out, only taken. Spec

Anyone can be shot, civilians included. Violence on a civilian that anyone sees moves Standing one step toward Menace, on top of the fight's own move (§04). A contact who witnesses it loses bravery and gains fear and resentment. Some turn Informer; more become Talkers who give you up when questioned (§04). It is the quickest way to undo everything you've built.

Violence has a price

The cost moves from the shot to the victim: +2 Trail for each person hit and +2 more if they go down, so dropping a guard costs 4 Trail. A silent takedown costs the same per person without the gunfire: a knockout +4 and a kill +6, charged when a report of it is confirmed or the victim gives a statement; a kill that is never found is a missing person (+2, §08). Any gunfire raises Alert to at least 2, and violence a civilian sees sets 3. Gunfire still calls the response unit, draws the rivals within 16 s, breaks the patrol within 30 m and moves Standing toward Menace if witnessed. Shooting a contact ends that relationship; shooting the target fails the mission. Shots in the final fight leave no Trail or Alert; shots before it count. Spec

History: the top-down test used a simpler version, superseded by the rules above. Each Enforcer shot took 6 s, two hits dropped a person or a patrol unit, the Enforcer could take three, and every shot added +1 Alert and +2 Trail. Built

The decisive shot

No first-person firefights (tiebreaker 5). Instead, once or twice per fight, time slows, the camera drops behind the Enforcer for one aimed shot (the rival leader, a police car's tyre), then returns to the tactical view. After capstone

07 · TRAINING MISSION · CAPSTONE

Handover

Councillor Vale signed the clearance order for the marked block. At shift handover he leaves the Civic Records Office for his official car. Take him alive to the getaway car. The whole cell is available and all four are armed (Arms 3), the purse is $100,000, and every verb is introduced once.

The top-down test in play at 2:39. The Scout has learned Inez’s debt, so the Fixer’s action cards show what each approach costs. Red cones are surveillance and security, amber is the guard, violet the rivals.

Layout and sightlines from the top-down test, which also supplied the art.

Casting. The mission names roles, not people: a café server on shift at the front door who is in debt, the councillor's official driver who needs cash, an Office guard who is a café regular, and the councillor. Each role is cast from the city's generated people and pinned by id; "Inez" and "Vale" are the only name parts written, and they go to whoever is cast. No mission authors a person. The Handover runs at security level 2, and the public fears its rival crew.

The heart of it: Inez and the guard are lovers. His café stop before his shift is to see her. "The guard comes to visit Inez when she calls him because you bribed / pressured her and that's what makes him leave his post" (Sky). Her debt is her need, which Help clears; the affair is her secret, which Pressure threatens to expose.

Schedule

0:00Vale is inside. The guard, cameras and patrol follow their routines. The cell stands loosely by the getaway car at the square's boarding pavilion, in view, and the camera opens on them.
1:00The door guard checks in, and again at 2:30, 4:00 and 5:30, the end of his shift. Other staff posts check in every 90 seconds from their own shift start.
3:10The rival car parks near the pickup.
5:40Last chance to turn the driver.
5:50Vale leaves by the north entrance, or the service lane if the driver was turned.
6:10Vale reaches the car.
8:30Rivals take Vale, or the official car leaves. Mission over.

Routes

A · Through the front door (before 5:50)

  1. Scout watches the café and listens to Inez (1:34).
  2. Fixer helps Inez by clearing her debt ($40,000).
  3. Tech loops the entrance camera (1:02) and stays tethered. Optionally, it reroutes the patrol for 1:55.
  4. Fixer calls Inez. The guard walks 30 s, stays 60 s and walks 30 s back: a 2:00 window. Payoff cut (§10).
  5. Enforcer enters (38 s), leaves with Vale by the service exit and heads for the car (44 s).

B · Take the pickup (from 5:50)

  1. Scout watches the official car: the driver needs cash (48 s).
  2. Fixer turns the driver before 5:40 ($40,000). The pickup moves to the service lane. Or the driver parks across the pickup camera for 2:30.
  3. Scout plants a false tip on the rivals (44 s), or you fight.
  4. Enforcer intercepts (38 s) and heads for the car (44 s).

G · Take the guard Spec

  1. Tech loops the entrance camera and reroutes the patrol.
  2. Scout watches the guard: his cone and his check-in marks.
  3. Enforcer knocks him out just after a mark, then leaves him, or carries him out of the door's sight if someone could find him while the cell still needs the door.
  4. Enforcer enters, leaves with Vale by the service door and heads for the car. About 3:36, $0, 6 Trail, Alert 1, and no guard at your side in the final fight.
  5. Or kill him and hide him in the lane's bin (before its round) or through the service door: cheaper now, but he becomes a missing person, the case stays open and the Office block hardens.

The driver can be taken too, by the same rules, but on the generated cast every chance is closed: by check-ins, by the shift change, or by Vale himself. Turn him instead (route B). The official car needs its driver; without one it waits. The Take: at Vale's own car with his driver turned, it happens inside the car, with nothing to see. Any other Take has a 5 s struggle onlookers can see, and Vale walked away on foot looks wrong only to his family, or to anyone within 3 m who sees the grip. Spec

The final fight: your approach picks your enemy Spec

Timings. Walking legs shorten where the cell runs, and the routes are retimed to match; the Enforcer walks while he carries Vale. Once Alert reaches 2, entering the Office takes 68 s (alarm inside, §05), and a door held over a found body can't be entered at all. Spec

Every run ends with a short fight on the way to the car, lasting 30–60 s with 3–5 hostiles. Its shots leave no Trail or Alert (§06).

You went loud

Any shot fired, or Alert 2 or higher. The police arrive from the north street (the top-down test's west street, as built) with 2–4 officers, joined by the response unit if it is already on the street, and the seal clock is running. There are no allies: the guard is down or against you.

You played it safe

No shots and Alert 1 or lower. The rival crew ambushes the extraction. The guard, who never saw you and was never taken down, fights the rivals attacking his post. A helped Inez warns you 10 s early. A turned driver blocks the rival car, so one fewer rival arrives. An earlier false tip cost them one more member.

Win and fail

Win: Vale reaches the getaway car alive.

08 · CAMPAIGN

From one waitress to the city

Act IOne personThe Fixer alone. Turn individuals, recruit the cell and build your first sources of income.
Act IINetworksContacts introduce contacts. Take over a workplace (the docks, a depot). Brave contacts fight beside you.

People are the economy Spec

A turned person can become a source that pays out every mission: a bank clerk skims cash, a quartermaster diverts arms, a café owner passes on tips that reveal needs before the Scout listens. Procurement missions target a source, not a one-off withdrawal. Resources turn more people, and more people produce more resources. This compounding is the snowball.

Wounds carry over Spec

Health doesn't reset between missions. A turned doctor heals the cell quickly and quietly. Without one, finding a doctor becomes an objective of its own: watch, turn or pay one before the main mission, if the city's calendar leaves time. Nothing forces it. Go in hurt, go in short-handed, or spend the days. The main mission's closing event keeps its date either way, because this is a living city, not a menu.

Objectives vary: a kidnapping, a bank job built on a planted teller, a killing by a manipulated proxy, a takeover won through a ruined reputation. Direct force always works, with a bigger trail. Spec

The risk is sameness. When everyone is generated, it's easy for nobody to be memorable. Watch Dogs: Legion is the cautionary example. 10 · PRESENTATION

Read the street at a glance

Camera

A tactical view from above (play zoom 14 at 38°, never first person) that turns in quarter steps, so yaw is 30, 120, 210 or 300, over a 3D city built from the district plan: DecoKit kit pieces where they count, procedural fill to the same bar. Target on-screen character height is 40–60 px at 1080p, enough to read job, silhouette and facing. The rules move across unchanged. Painted plates are at most an optional extra after the capstone. With several levels, architecture above the selected person's level ghosts to 0.2 and keeps 0.4 of its shadow, so the street behind a faded tower is lit and the tower still marks the ground. The mission opens with the camera framed on the cell.

Views: the opening view is yaw 30. The Records Office front is played at yaw 210, two quarter turns from the opening view: the public door, its approach, South walkway, patrol-b, the patrol sweep, the cabinet, the service lane and the service door are all in view there (at yaw 30 the public door is behind the Office's wings and shows only through the fade). The visibility rule V-1 measures each mission point from the heading it is played at, past architecture and without the fade: 45 of the Handover's 47 points are clear, and the two left hidden, Behind café (the Scout's seat) and patrol-reroute, are hidden by design.

Built world or live state

Built world (generated from the plan at build time, fixed in play): buildings, paving, structures, street furniture, skyline. Live 3D state: people, vehicles, doors, surveillance, barricades, posters, and anything that changes state. Both share one material and lighting standard; match lighting on one character and one vehicle before building more.

Control and time

Left click selects an agent or moves the selection (Shift adds); drag a box to select. Right click a person or object to open the action panel: every action the cell can take on that target, grouped by agent, each with its full price, and locked rows saying why. With a verb picked on 1–4, a right click fires it directly; a right click on empty ground cancels. Double-click runs; G, or a click on an agent's walk/run glyph, switches a moving agent between walk and run. A moving agent's destination shows as a numbered pin, and Alt shows the walk paths. With the Enforcer, a right click on a person offers Knock out and Kill. Hold Alt for detail; I opens Intel, L or the notes key the history, R the response list, H hides hints. The briefing (until Begin) and the end card are modal: nothing in the street answers the mouse or keys under them. Buttons carry no key labels; a key is taught by the hint the first time it matters. WASD, the arrow keys or a middle-drag pan, and the wheel zooms within the 40–60 px limit. Q and E turn the view 90° about the ground at the centre of the screen; Alt + middle-drag turns it freely and snaps to the nearest quarter on release; the plot scope turns with the view, with a north wedge on its rim. F1–F4, a portrait click or Tab selects an agent, and a double-tap centres on them. Space pauses, = and − change speed, and N jumps to the next event. In a fight, F draws or holsters; with weapons drawn, a right click on a hostile fires until they are down (hold and sweep to switch target); X ceases fire, V cycles the stance, Ctrl is needed to fire on a civilian or contact, and both buttons together is the panic order. Every binding is remappable from one table. Real time is the default; the tactical pause is a tool (T1 tests it). The same orders always give the same result, so pausing never changes the outcome.

Readability

Surveillance cones in security red, the guard in amber, rivals in violet. Signals are drawn unlit and emissive and outside the post grade, so neither light nor grade shifts them: a signal never depends on the light. Each has its own shape or motion cue, so it reads by shape, not by owning its colour: red, amber and violet are free for the world and props (Sky, 16 October). Intel replaces the dossier: the mission's key people as discs, filled once known, with name, job, need and temperament as icons; the sentences are on Alt. Kills are shown: the act plays on screen and the body lies where it fell. Fights read at a glance: a tracer for every shot, a miss that ends past the target and never on the body, health pips over everyone in a fight, crosshair ticks for the range band (a shape, not a colour) and a cross when there is no line, a stance icon on the portrait, a thin 13 m ring round a runner while running is noticed, and the going-loud card with its held commit.

HUD: less reading, built for real time

No sentences in play, except people speaking. "It's the reading, it's too much" (Sky). Everything else is an icon, a number, a ring or a line, and the rules show in the street. Spec

  • At rest: the roster of four portraits (health pips, an inner ring on the selected one, a busy chip with the act's glyph, a bar and the seconds left, and the walk/run glyph while moving) · the selected agent's order plate (1–4) · the status pill (clock, pause, the next mark with "?" while unknown, cash, Trail, Alert) · the known-people discs under the pill · the plot scope, bottom left · the notes key, bottom right, with an unread dot · at most two icons over a person. The look is Glyph's round 4 v10 signage kit with the roster in the left column, closed as built; the dock stays a setting.
  • Lines: one goal line at the bottom centre, an imperative with its key noun in its marker's colour ("Take ▼Vale alive."), shown for 6 s and again at the chime and when Vale comes out; the hint shares its place and retires once you have used its verb. Story beats only, lower right, at most two, four words or fewer ("Inez called the guard.", "Body found.", "Police coming."). Speech bubbles at the speaker. A refusal is one pop: an icon and a few words ("Too far · 4 m", "Watch first").
  • World markers, for what the cell knows: an eye (open, shut or ?) over a watcher and over a takedown's target · a ring on a knocked-out body that empties as he comes round · a lock on a held door · a "!" and a dotted line for a witness walking to a phone · a clock pip over a watched guard, counting to his next check-in · cones you have learned, one at a time, all of them on Alt · hiding-place plates, a carry disc, unit badges, objective marks and edge arrows.
  • The plot scope ("Minimap may be the key though. For example knowing where Vale is located is not obvious", Sky): a period plotting scope that shows only what the cell knows. The cell; Vale's last known place as a ring that grows with the age of the news, exact only while someone sees him; the key people once met; learned cones and the patrol route; held doors, bodies, hiding places, reports on their way and units arriving. Edge arrows point to Vale and to anything urgent. You pan and select from it, but give no orders.
  • Alt, held: every learned mark at once, names over known people, every field of every price, and the long lines.
  • A budget, checked on every capture: the HUD covers at most 15 % of the screen at rest (aim under 10 %), 22 % with an order card open and 30 % with Alt, with no running text outside speech, beats and the goal line. A new mechanic says how it reads without text before it is built.

The price before you commit, in real time

Every order still shows its full price before you commit. One line per way: the verb, then only the fields that aren't zero, in a fixed order: cash, time (the walk and the act as one number), Trail, Alert, an eye (seen, unseen, or ? for a watcher not yet watched), what it teaches, the pace of a carry, and whether it will work (✓, ✗, ½ or ?). A takedown marks the numbers that apply only if the body is found: "Knock out · 7 s · (found) +4 · ▲1". Alt shows the rest. The move ring: where you point on the ground, a ring answers instead of a chip: turquoise with footprints when nothing will see the walk, the watcher's colour with an open eye when something will (the exposed stretch of the route glows), cream and dashed with a "?" eye when a watcher on the way is unknown, and a dark double ring with the alarm lamp when the move raises Alert. Its rim fills with the walk time; Alt adds the numbers. The going-loud card: the first order that would make a run loud (drawing where someone will see, firing before a fight is on, the panic order with no fight) opens a card of icons and numbers at the cursor: Alert to 2, or 3 with the civilians watching; who comes and when; the seal time; what the final fight loses; and +2 Trail for each person hit and each person dropped. You commit by holding the same input for half a second while the game keeps running; releasing or Esc cancels. The card never appears once a fight is on. After it, only a small chip per target.

Payoff cuts

When a plan lands, cut briefly to a street-level camera before returning to the same state. The capstone guarantees one: Inez spills the coffee and the guard walks off. More payoff cuts and the decisive shot come later. Spec

Audio is part of the clock

  • Routines you can hear: a bell, the café door, the handover chime at 5:30.
  • Security warns before it acts: a surveillance click at the edge of each sweep, and a change in the patrol's sound when it breaks route.
  • Alert adds layers to the music. A fight brings in the whole score. Contacts confirm calls aloud.
  • Each weapon has its own voice, so you can hear who is firing, and police dispatch sounds from the north street, so you hear where they come from.

Look: retro-future, held in the art bible

A bright retro-future city: a 1952–1962 space age imagined as the present, built as high art. It is an alternate history, not a forecast (section 01): a 1950s world that discovered atomic power centuries ago, so its culture and style are the 1950s and its technology is centuries ahead, with no thinking machines or networks. The design test for every object is 1950s style with centuries-ahead technology. A pastel base of cream and peach limestone with saturated enamel accents (cobalt, flamingo, sunshine, mint, turquoise) on panels, awnings, signs, roofs and trim, lagoon water, coral transit, chrome, and a skyline of towers, rockets and planets. It is optimistic on the surface and coercive underneath, and that contrast sets the tone. Citizens wear space-age couture as street clothing, never 1950s period dress: people prompts carry no era date, since dates pulled character concepts into Americana (v0.6.1, and Sky again at v0.20.1); security and institutions dress sleeker in ivory, black, gold and chrome; robots are characters with dot-matrix faces, 1950s in style and clockwork-smart on fixed routines. The four in the cell look like visitors from a nearby timeline: the same world a few decades on, sharper and cleaner, so they pass in the street and still stand out at 50 px. The captures below are the reference. In play, the skyline and distant views frame the edge of the screen while the playable block stays dense and tactical.

The look is set; the palette is current and tuneable. Agent GDD §15 and its machine copy, contracts/style/suborned.style.json (v0.21.0, wins on conflict), hold the palette with hex values, materials, finishes, the hard rules, the reference board and the probe set any new render route must pass. The world palette comes from unity/Assets/Suborned/Editor/World/looks/harbour.json. Since v0.23.0 the signal colours are not reserved: red, amber and violet are free for the world, and signals stay readable by their unlit draw and their own shape or motion. Tuned in the world for v0.18.0: lagoon water #3d8d93, canvas #f7f4ec, and facade accent roles in teal, coral, gold, mint and peach. For v0.19.0 the world gold turns to brass #99784d at street level and on facades (below). Sky reviews it in the world and it can still be tuned. The v0.15.0 art bible is history: a concept look reference, superseded on presentation and palette. Vela, Forma, Glint and Glyph hold §15.

The Harbour District skyline. SpaceHQ is the city's flagship and centrepiece at Crown Circus: the tallest thing in the district, about 252 m, a fluted cream-and-gold tower crowned with an atom over a needle mast, not a rocket. Rival spires stand inland and may be taller than the Skyport (123–194 m, never more than 200); the Skyport, at 108 m, is the harbour's icon, and nothing within 150 m of the quay is taller. Crown Avenue keeps its tower heights, the needle at 167.8 m and the avenue gates at 165.6 m, an exception to the massing grammar's 20 % height variety. Rockets stand only on the horizon, at least 3.2 km out. The sky rail threads buildings and megastructures through portals, and stations also sit inside buildings at the sky concourse. The Parade stays open to the sky: the sky rail passes through the gate block's portal, and glazed barrel canopies run over the side gallery promenades only, never over the carriageway or the play space, so the tactical camera sees the street, its sun and shadows, and the full skyline. The ocean liner at the berth is concept B, "atomic": a flared white hull with a coral boot-top and a gold sheer line, a domed glass observation lounge at the bow, twin swept-back coral tail-fin funnels and a chrome radar mast topped by an atom.

The civic block and the street. The eight concept paintings of 26 September 2026 (briefs/008/concepts/, hashes in PROVENANCE.json) are the reference for the civic block and for the street-level character of the district: cream stone, seafoam teal bands, chrome spheres, banners, planted terraces, pale paving with teal bands, cypress and palms, parasol terraces. The skyline keeps its own reference, the AtomicAge and Blocks sheets. The 30 September capstone concept and its testbed models are not the reference, though their dressing parts may be reused. On the civic block, seafoam #72b5a7 and deep teal #1f6c67 are the kit enamels, with civic wall ivory #eee9da, pale seafoam #9bcfc2 and brass trim #99784d. Banners, flowers and any tram take the palette's coral, flamingo or peach, or, since v0.23.0, the paintings' red-orange. Brass, not gold, at street level and on facades: brass #99784d and light brass #ad866f; a lighter brass is now allowed too, picked from concept art. The skyline crowns keep their gold (#e3d681, #c9c08e) until a far shot decides. Gold or brass stays hairline, frame, bead and small metal. A large part never takes brass or gold; it takes an enamel, chrome or stone role: the rooftop spheres keep their building's enamel, as roof parts take their host building's enamel pair and the paintings show chrome and pearl spheres, and the two areas that listed gold (lantern and records) take sunshine #f8e26c. Crossings have no landing slab since brief 009 (below), so the landing colour pick is closed; the look role crossing retires when the generator change lands.

Concept art first. "Everything should come from concept art really": look decisions come from concept art generated from an open brief in the world's style ("let the AI concept art come up with its own design"). The ΔE and checker rules gate what the art proposes; they are not the source of options. Every concept generation starts from the style contract's concept_prompt: the era (section 01's premise), the city line of the prompts Sky accepted (briefs/009/concepts/PROVENANCE.json), an avoid list and the rule. A decision taken from art cites the image and its prompt. The tools are the Codex CLI image tool (ChatGPT plan) and Runware (Qwen Image 2.1).

Crossings, as this world builds them. The concepts in briefs/009/concepts/ are the reference. Floating signal orbs ("I do like those eyes"): chrome orbs or small saucers hover over the kerb at each end of a crossing, with a round display on each face showing a walking figure (the stop figure may be red) and a thin beam down to a glowing disc on the paving where people wait. No zebra, no paint, no landing slab: the crossing is light set flush in the road, glowing seafoam bars or rows of light dots in brass frames, with brass dome studs along the kerb edge and seafoam inlay arcs in the paving where the crossing lands. In the browser build: the Handover café from the tactical camera and Inez at street level (the view a payoff cut uses). In Unity: a populated DecoKit plaza.

A reskin is still possible. If the city moves to another era, that era must provide: institutions that watch people (cameras, watchmen, informants or switchboards) for the Tech to blind · motor vehicles and dense crowds · jobs you can read from clothing · a respectable surface over a coercive machine · firearms and a plausible way to rig a vehicle.

11 · BUILD

Prove the rules small, then dress them

Built

  • Top-down test of Handover: four operatives, two contacts, security, rivals, shooting, debrief and campaign lock. 28 scenario tests pass.
  • Harbour District 3D world in progress, built from the plan: world generator and export, DecoKit kit pieces plus procedural fill, Unity builder. Handover goes in next, then player actions.
  • City simulation architecture chosen: one C# engine as a Unity-free library.

How it's built

  • The rules live apart from the engine. Everything that happens in the city (a guard leaving, a contact answering) is an event with its conditions, effects and witnesses.
  • Any run can be replayed exactly from its starting state and the player's orders.
  • Unity has to pass the same 28 scenarios as the top-down test before it's trusted.
  • One simulation engine. A Unity-free C# library: Unity runs it live, build tools run it headless. Fixed 10 Hz tick, integer state; a replay is the orders plus checksums.
  • Performance is judged by frame rate at play zoom, not by polygon counts. The target is 60 fps at 1080p on a 15-inch MacBook Air M4 (Mac16,13), the reference machine. It has no fan and a 10-core GPU, so it is measured warm, after several minutes of running, at play zoom with people, vehicles and the simulation in, by a perf harness in a development build. A mid-range PC (an RTX 3060-class GPU with a 6-core CPU) must also pass, as a check, not the bar.

One rulebook for everyone. Seventeen agents stay consistent because they all build against one list of everything that can happen in the city: what each event needs, what it changes and who sees it. Keel keeps that list. Playtest and QA lead · SutureThe build, the scenario, the expected outcome and the questions to ask playersA test report with steps to reproduce, what should and did happen, and clips. Runs uncoached playtests, sends bugs to their owners and retests.

Specialist handoffs

AgentGive them → expect back
Dialogue designer · FableMotive's temperament rules and each person's state → a dialogue generator whose lines match what that person can do and how they feel (brave, bitter, promoted). Motive reviews; Latch builds it in.

Glyph checks legibility.

Decisions (v0.24.0)

  • Sky (17 October, "yeah, camera rotation"; brief 016): the view turns in quarter steps with Q and E (yaw 30, 120, 210, 300), Alt + middle-drag snaps to the nearest, and the plot scope turns heading-up; the view opens at yaw 30. This replaces v0.22.0's "camera rotation is rejected for now: yaw stays 30" and takes rotation off the parked list; third person stays parked. It is view only: rules, scenarios and replays are untouched.
  • Sky (18 October, "yeah try H"; Vantage's re-study, briefs/011/vantage/door-recheck.json, h-door-210.png, rot-door-four.png): keep the civic block as built and play the Records Office front at yaw 210. At yaw 30 the camera sees only the Office's south face (the official door) and west face (the service door, brief 013); the public door is behind 15.5 m wings and shows only through the fade. At 210 the door, its approach, South walkway, patrol-b, the patrol sweep, the cabinet, the service lane and the service door are all in view. V-1 measures each point from the heading it is played at: 45 of 47 are clear, and Behind café (the Scout's seat) and patrol-reroute are hidden by design. Rejected: (b) the public door on the west face, 1 m from the service door and watching the quiet lane; (d) the paintings' layout, a full rebuild and worse at the other three headings.

Decisions (v0.23.0)

  • Sky (brief 013): anyone can be targeted, with no list; the cost comes from who sees it. Bodies stay where they fall and are found; the Enforcer carries them to a quiet place, outdoors or through a service door. Both knockout and kill: someone knocked out talks unless hidden, tied up or turned; someone killed never talks, but a found body is far worse. Kills are shown. The cones are the Scout's skill.
  • Sky, answering Motive: a killing found moves Standing −1, as one value to tune; no rule finds every body, so a hidden one is a missing person (+2 Trail, no Menace, the family and workmates worry; one more guard and camera on that block for 3 missions; every 2 open cases raise the district's security level; a found killing's case closes after 3 missions); the Enforcer's face is a fact a Talker can give up; guards check in every 90 s at times the Scout can learn; a service door and a bin in the lane; the driver can be taken, a missing expected person raises the alarm, and an alarm sends robots and police to the scene and to the connections; the response's size and speed are the difficulty dial, kept as data.
  • Sky ("otherwise ok to others", the merged calls): Alert rises when a silent act's report lands; a knockout never raises Alert above 1; the dial has five levels and the Handover is level 2; Mercenaries keep quiet until Alert 2; turned witnesses add no Trail; a body is either open or hidden; call boxes are placed by a world rule; the Tech can't cut them; bins are emptied only within the mission; kills are shown.
  • Sky: a found body locks down the scene (doors in sight held, no entry); a Take at Vale's own car with his driver turned happens inside the car; preparation earns the right to leave a body.
  • Sky (brief 014): turning conversations are private, except Pressure; Standing leans Hero, starting at +2, with word of mouth and drift (Motive's note: "sure"); a public fight moves Standing once, by who you fought, and breaking feared rivals is +1; less reading, rules 1–12 ("a good starting point"); the minimap; one waitress outside the café while customers come and go; the cell starts in view.
  • Sky (in play, 16 October): G switches walk and run; destination pins replace the route line, with the paths on Alt; the notes key sits bottom right; the briefing and end card are modal; no key labels on buttons; a colour-coded ring with a symbol replaces the chip at the cursor.
  • Sky: signal colours are not reserved. Signals stay readable by being drawn unlit and emissive, each with its own shape or motion cue.
  • Sky (17 October, on brief 015: "yeah, all good - move forwards on the gdd and we'll iterate if need to"): the 22 crew-made rules listed in briefs/015-gdd-v0.23.md are kept, among them the Enforcer alone taking people down, telling someone indoors only by phone, one dispatch per incident, the witness reactions, the dial's numbers, the alarm reaching the raiser's people too, and the public fight's −1 cases. The move ring is Glyph's variant A; takedown prices keep the "found" mark; a price's time is the walk and the act together; the HUD's dock and finish are closed as built; banners may take the paintings' red-orange and brass may go lighter; the final fight lasts 30–60 s, as the rulebook has it; Intel replaces the dossier; the rivals' public standing is set per mission for now, with a district default later, with the campaign.
  • Parked, not in this version: camera rotation and a third-person try-out (Sky wants both; mechanics come first, and nothing about sight may assume a fixed yaw); the raygun as the Fixer's sidearm; the Enforcer calling in his own contacts early to hold positions (later missions).
  • Corrections (Aster): v0.22.0 listed Inez's affair as parked. It never was: "I never parked Inez's link — that's the whole capstone" (Sky, 15 October); section 07 now carries it. The v0.18.0, v0.19.0 and v0.20.0 entries credit the ΔE 20 signal-colour gate to Sky. Sky asked for unlit, emissive signals with a shape or motion cue, and for red on displays; the colour reservation itself was the crew's, and Sky dropped it on 16 October ("That red for signals rule isn't something I requested though").

Decisions (v0.22.0)

  • Sky: "more realtime than strategy". Real-time play is the default and pause is a tool, not the mode. Commander, not avatar and preparation beats improvisation stay tiebreakers (section 01).
  • Sky, on Motive's running and shoot-out proposal (briefs/011/motive-fights.md): the whole cell is armed, limited by Arms; running is 2.8 m/s; the Enforcer can't run while carrying Vale; the going-loud card is committed by a half-second hold, with no pause; entering takes 30 s longer once Alert reaches 2. Its changes go into sections 02, 03, 05, 06, 07 and 10, with a new test, T8: can players say why an operative went down? Fights stay "not a separate combat game": fast, real-time and Syndicate-like, still measuring preparation; the cost moves from the shot to the person hit.
  • Sky (brief 011 balance, briefs/011/motive-balance.md; already in the engine): Watch takes 20 s, not 52; the Handover closes at 8:30, not 8:00, with the waitress's shift running to the close; shots in the final fight add no Trail or Alert, so a quiet route can end Calm, while loud shots before it still count.
  • Sky: the controls for real time (briefs/011/play/HOW-TO-PLAY.md and Motive's fight controls) replace "click to select or move, Shift to group, 1–4 operative, E engage, F fire, C call, click a person for the action card" (section 10). Camera rotation is rejected for now: yaw stays 30.
  • Sky: the HUD is simple and Syndicate-style, built for real time (briefs/011/ui/round4 v10, round5, round5/placement): roster, verb plate, status pill, price chip, at most two icons over a person, the action panel. The dock is a setting; the default dock (left column or corner) and the finish (cab-cluster or deco-console) are still Sky's open pick.
  • Sky: "every order shows its full price before you commit" stays. In real time it is met by the price chip on hover, the action panel, the run price on ground hover and the going-loud card.
  • Aster: section 07's "west street" was the top-down test's compass; as built, the police come in by the north street (contracts/missions/handover/mission.json), as Motive's proposal reads.
  • Parked, not in this version: Inez's affair and the story canon; changes to the cell's look rules (undecided); camera rotation.

Decisions (v0.21.0)

  • Sky: the city's people are generated through the build-time pipeline with SurrealDB retrieval, from their placements and routines. The model writes cast tables and seeded code makes the people, never one model answer per person. Mission people are city people, cast by role and pinned by id. The civic block goes first, then the district.
  • Sky, on Motive's Dwarf Fortress study (briefs/010/research/): no alias for the cell yet, it is known by face; a met need is replaced between missions; the preview shows the price always and the outcome as "?" until the temperament is known; the wrong approach works one step worse and a refused one fails; investigators question simulated people only; news along ties is facts, never opinion; the named steps, the rule that every field is read, the temperament mix, introductions along ties and the knowledge start state go into sections 04 and 09.
  • Aster (Motive's people rules, in force through the accepted cast; Sky may strike any): loyalty in the Talker test is loyalty to the cell; Idealists start braver and the Fearful start uneasy; nine needs; the tie kinds and limits; restricted temperaments for guards, patrol, investigators, councillors, watchers and creditors; one district name pool of at least six origins with no 1950s-Americana names; the corner café is the diner trade.
  • Sky: the first civic-block cast (people runs r012 and r013, $1.82 of a $3 ceiling) is accepted and promoted to contracts/people/, and the Handover's four roles are pinned to its people.
  • Sky: every crew member can search and read the web, because the GDD can't cover a project this complex. Anything that shapes a decision is saved with its sources in briefs/<n>/research/; the pipeline's model calls stay without tools.

Decisions (v0.20.1)

  • Sky: "too strong a 1950s ruined character concept". It happened at v0.6.1, when dates in the era pulled the first people sheets into 1950s Americana. The 1950s of the premise belongs to places, objects and machines; people, character, lineup, model and versions prompts never carry it and start from the style contract's dateless era and its couture line. People painted into a place frame (the fedoras and tea dresses in briefs/009/concepts/) are not costume reference (style contract concept_prompt.people).

Decisions (v0.20.0)

  • Sky: the world is an alternate history, not a forecast: "a 1950s world that discovered atomic power centuries ago" ("retro future was 1950's but if the world had discovered atomic power hundreds years ago"; "robots have 1950's style, the trams etc, just the technology is super advanced"). It replaces "the 1950s imagining the year 2000" of brief 007's image prompts. Atomic power made energy, travel and building cheap, and everything physical is abundant. Thinking machines and networks never came ("internet wasn't a thing"): robots are clockwork-smart on fixed routines, records are physical, and information moves through people and paper, so people are the weak point. The city fears disorder most, which is the reason for its optimistic surface and coercive machinery. The design test for every object: 1950s style, centuries-ahead technology.
  • Aster: both GDDs and the style contract were checked against the premise, with no hard contradiction. The clear compatible readings are recorded in section 01: closed-circuit cameras watched by people, a watcher's log as a physical record, calls as voice between people, the "networks" as people and transit lines, and the AI terms as build terms ("no AI during play" stays a build rule). Readings that would change a rule went to Sky as questions.
  • Sky: red is allowed on electronic displays ("red is definitely ok for electronics displays"). A small emissive display pictogram, such as a crossing signal's stop figure, may be red; it is never a surface, and the cones keep their own shape and motion cue. It is an exception to the ΔE 20 signal-colour rule for display pictograms only.
  • Sky: concept art first ("everything should come from concept art really"; "let the AI concept art come up with its own design"). Look decisions come from concept art generated from an open brief in the world's style; the ΔE and checker rules gate what the art proposes and are not the source of options. The tools are the Codex CLI image tool (ChatGPT plan) and Runware (Qwen Image 2.1). Every concept generation starts from the style contract's concept_prompt, whose city line is the prompts Sky accepted (briefs/009/concepts/PROVENANCE.json); a decision taken from art cites the image and its prompt.
  • Sky (brief 009): crossings as this world builds them, with briefs/009/concepts/ as the reference. Floating signal orbs ("I do like those eyes"): chrome orbs or small saucers over the kerb at each end, a round display on each face with a walking figure, a thin beam down to a glowing disc where people wait. No zebra, no paint, no landing slab: light set flush in the road (glowing seafoam bars or rows of light dots) in brass frames, brass dome studs along the kerb edge, seafoam inlay arcs where the crossing lands. The landing surface of v0.19.0 goes with the slab, so its colour pick is closed.
  • Fact (brief 008): the reference machine measured is the 15-inch MacBook Air M4 (Mac16,13).

Decisions (v0.19.0)

  • Sky: the eight concept paintings of 26 September 2026 (briefs/008/concepts/, hashes in PROVENANCE.json) are the reference for the civic block and the street-level character of the district: cream stone, seafoam teal bands, chrome spheres, banners, planted terraces, pale paving with teal bands, cypress and palms, parasol terraces. The skyline keeps the AtomicAge and Blocks sheets of brief 007. The 30 September capstone concept and its testbed models are not the reference; their dressing parts may be reused.
  • Sky: on the civic block, seafoam #72b5a7 and deep teal #1f6c67 are the kit enamels, with civic wall ivory #eee9da, pale seafoam #9bcfc2 and civic trim brass #99784d. Banners, flowers and any tram take the palette's coral, flamingo or peach, never the paintings' red-orange (ΔE 8.8 from the cones signal).
  • Sky: brass, not gold, at street level and on facades ("I prefer brass to gold"): brass #99784d and light brass #ad866f, the lightest brass that holds ΔE 20 from the guard; a lighter, yellower brass drifts onto the guard amber. The skyline crowns keep their gold (#e3d681, #c9c08e) until a far shot decides. Gold or brass stays hairline, frame, bead and small metal only; a large part never takes brass or gold; it takes an enamel, chrome or stone role (the rooftop spheres keep their building's enamel; the two areas that listed gold, lantern and records, take sunshine #f8e26c). The paintings show chrome and pearl spheres, and roof parts take their host building's enamel pair. Crossing landings have their own surface; its colour is Sky's open pick (mint #7fd0b8 recommended; #d0c848 today).
  • Sky: Crown Avenue keeps its tower heights: the needle at 167.8 m and the avenue gates at 165.6 m, 13.6 % and 14.8 % under the starburst, an exception to the massing grammar's 20 % height variety. The plan does not change; checker rule K-2 holds every regenerated tower to the tip its order states.
  • Aster: signals also draw outside the post grade, since the grade shifts them ΔE 4–10 (Glint measured the guard 19.0 from shaded stone). A signal must never depend on the light: the fix is the signal, never a darker street. Glyph specifies, Latch builds.
  • Aster (Glint's value): the architecture fade's ghost keeps 0.4 of its shadow, separate from the ghost's own 0.2, so the street behind a faded tower is lit and the tower still marks the ground. Glint tunes it.

Decisions (v0.18.0)

  • Sky: signals (cones, guard and rival markers) render unlit and emissive, each with its shape or motion cue. The ΔE 20 gate applies to the unlit palette against the signal colours.
  • Sky: the performance target is 60 fps at 1080p on a MacBook Air M4, the reference machine (no fan, 10-core GPU), measured warm at play zoom with people, vehicles and the simulation in, by a perf harness in a development build. A mid-range PC (an RTX 3060-class GPU with a 6-core CPU) must also pass, as a check. This replaces the PC-only target set earlier the same day in brief 007: the play camera sees a small slice of the city, so integrated graphics is the bar.
  • Sky: SpaceHQ is the city's flagship and centrepiece at Crown Circus (about 252 m), crowned with an atom over a needle mast, not a rocket. Rockets stay on the horizon, at least 3.2 km out. Spires may be taller than the Skyport: inland rivals reach 123–194 m, while the Skyport (108 m) is the harbour's icon and nothing within 150 m of the quay is taller.
  • Sky: the sky rail threads buildings through portals, and stations also sit inside buildings at the sky concourse.
  • Sky: the Parade stays open to the sky. The sky rail passes through the gate block's portal; glazed barrel canopies run over the side gallery promenades only, never over the carriageway or the play space.
  • Sky: the ocean liner is concept B, "atomic". It replaces the liner that read as a modern cruise ship. Owner: Vela.
  • Sky: the palette is tuned in the world: lagoon water #3d8d93, gold #d0c848, canvas #f7f4ec, and accent roles in teal, coral, gold, mint and peach.

Decisions (v0.17.0)

  • Sky: presentation is 3D. The world is a real city built from the plan; painted plates are at most an optional extra. The camera stays fixed and tactical.
  • Sky: the palette mixes a pastel cream and peach base with saturated enamel accents. It is the current palette and can be tuned once seen in the world.
  • Aster: the DecoKit generator belongs to Vela (pieces, materials, facade detail), with Splice owning the pipeline.
  • Aster: Keel builds and owns the C# simulation library; Latch hosts it in Unity; Redline reviews. Open for Sky: confirm, or have Latch build it to Keel's spec.
  • Aster: Splice keeps the checks and the plan-to-world pipeline. The people and vehicle generator moves to Pulse and the mission rule overlays to Waymark: designers own their generators.

The city is planned before it is dressed: Datum lays out the district and Vantage each block, and Latch builds only a plan that passes, so art dresses a city that already works. Motive and Keel draft the rulebook first, and everyone else works from that draft in parallel while Latch builds the game. The week 3 and 4 playtests can still change the rules, so the rulebook is locked only after week 4.

Budget. Agent work runs inside two existing 20× subscriptions (one Codex, one Claude), which cap usage over time rather than charging per use. Aster watches both and drops optional work when the allowance runs low. Anything paid per use, such as Runware and Meshy credits, is priced before use.

contracts/missions/handover/mission.json.text:
{
 "schema": "suborned.mission/3",
 "id": "handover",
 "note": "The Handover mission layer, moved out of the world: destinations and crew (block frame, from the old handover-block.json, suborned.block/2), the plan routes (getaway, official), and the rules that read them (C-3 mission points land on a plot or street, M-1 routes reach their end, W-1 walk origins from standards.walking.from). The world holds none of it. Input to brief 003. Run: bun tools/plan/cli.ts --overlay tools/missions/handover/overlay.ts. suborned.mission/2 (2026-10-14) adds the schedule the world's life rules held until Pulse regenerated them: status, clock, timeline, events, stands. Re-sited 2026-10-14 (Waymark; brief 008 B2, Vantage): the Records Office doors now stand on its tower faces, so four door points follow them. Office entrance (54.65, -30.5) to (51.75, -30), on the public landing 0.75 m up six steps; Office approach (52, -30.5) to (48.6, -30), at the foot of those steps; Official entrance and Meet Vale (73.25, -31) to (76.25, -30), the flush official door under the canopy.  "schema": "suborned.text/1",

 "author": "Fable (brief 011; GDD v0.22.0 §04, §07, §09, §10, §14)",
 "gdd": "the-suborned-agent-gdd-v0.22.0-2026-10-15.md",
 "rule": "The words of the Handover, made at build time and read by the Unity host; nothing here is written live and no line decides anything (GDD §09: text is a light layer, history is what the systems record). The host finds a line with lookup() and picks a variant with pickIndex() (contracts/missions/handover/text.schema.ts): same seed and same run, same words. Keys follow the engine: verbs are the panel verb ids, outcomes the rulebook outcomes (`suspicious` when the person reports the approach), refusals are text codes found by lockOf() because the engine returns free text. People are named only Inez and Vale; everyone else is a role. Civilians are never the payload: no line asks a civilian to die, fight or be used as a weapon. Lines that name Halcyon are pending Sky (a Story proposal): ship the `unnamed` cliffhanger until Sky decides. Inez and the door guard are lovers (the Story spine; Sky, 2026-10-15): her debt is her need (Help), her secret is the guard (Pressure threatens to expose it). Written plainly and with tact, never explicit.",
 "tone": {
  "world": "An alternate 1950s that found atomic power centuries ago: 1950s manners and speech, centuries-ahead machines, no thinking machines or networks. Optimistic on the surface, coercive underneath: the city is polite, orderly and watching. Speech is plain, short and spoken; no period slang to dress it up, no modern internet speech.",
  "voices": {
   "scout": "terse and observant: fragments, what is where, counts and positions; never warm, never wrong",
   "fixer": "warm and persuasive: reassures, says \"we\", puts people at ease; steel under the kindness",
   "tech": "calm and practical: procedure, minutes and what is tied to what; patient, a little dry about old wiring",
   "enforcer": "dry, older, few words: one to four words where he can; gallows humour, never a speech",
   "waitress": "Inez: warm café patter, quick, tired about money and the lender; her temperament shows in what she will and won't take",
   "driver": "Vale's official driver: gruff and practical; cars, wages, schedules; calls Vale \"the Councillor\"",
   "guard": "the door guard: officialese, clipped, the post and the rules; a mercenary one talks bonuses and \"off the clock\"",
   "councillor": "Vale: formal and pompous, then frightened; loyal blusters, mercenary bargains, fearful begs",
   "rivals": "cold and businesslike: a contract, a schedule, no names",
   "patrol": "a clockwork patrol: fixed polite phrases that mean orders (\"Walking is encouraged. Running is reported.\")",
   "security": "the response unit: crisp, loud, procedural",
   "watcher": "a person in the camera room, speaking into a handset: reports what the camera shows",
   "crowd": "passers-by: startled, short, human; they never fight and are never used"
  },

 "cards": {
  "rule": "The feed's cards for engine events no scene covers (Sky's review 2026-10-16, messages.html §1 D). Each is a title and one result in the player's words with the engine's numbers, never the engine's sentence (its log keeps that). A card with `sight` shows only when an agent can see the place, as a city scene does. A result that is a record is chosen by the engine state `pick` names. {who} is the person or watcher as names.targets says it, {agent} \"the Scout\"; the host capitalises the first letter after filling. Brief 013 (takedowns): a card says only what the cell has seen or been told. Three kinds: (1) the cell's own acts (the agent is there, so no `sight`); (2) things at a place the cell may not be near: `sight` in-sight, and `at` names the engine position the check looks at (the log carries none; the host reads it from the game); (3) the city's answer to an Alert, which the Alert pill and the street show: a card says that it came and when, never who made the report or why. `needs` routine: a cause the cell can name only once a Watch has taught the person's routine (a missed check in); until then report.landed speaks alone. Codes the engine builds (stash.container, stash.door) are one card keyed by the prefix. A spoken line of an event shows with that event's card or scene, so it follows the same sight rule: a line is never shown when its card is hidden. Brief 014 (less reading): every card has a `fate`: beat (a one-line feed beat, `beat`; at most ten distinct lines in the file), icon (the street shows it: a marker, ring, lock or pip), alt (history only, behind L), debrief (the end says it). A card with no beat is never a card on screen; its title and result are the history lines.",

  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"turned","temperament":"loyal","lines":["You stood by me. I'll stand by you.","The owner would approve. Count me in."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"kept","temperament":"loyal","lines":["You keep your word. So will I.","Steady of you. I notice."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Even a favour gets reported, I'm afraid.","Kind or not, I have to write it down."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"turned","temperament":"idealist","lines":["You'd tell the Office about us? Fine.","That's cruel. I'll do it. Once."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"idealist","lines":["Threats? I'll tell everyone I know.","You'll be reported, you and your threats."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"turned","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["All right, all right. No need to be nasty.","Business, then. Keep our secret. I'll do it."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"turned","temperament":"fearful","lines":["Please. Don't tell. I'll do whatever you say.","Yes! Yes. Just keep it secret. Please."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"waitress","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["I'll tell the owner exactly what you said.","A threat? That goes in the book."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"driver","outcome":"refused","temperament":"idealist","lines":["Give me a reason, not a favour.","Ask me why first. Then ask again."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"idealist","lines":["If it keeps people in their homes, yes.","For the block? Count me in."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"idealist","lines":["Careful. I could tell the Office.","Don't ask that here. People report."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"driver","outcome":"refused","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["Nothing for nothing. Bring cash next time.","My time's paid for. Yours isn't."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"driver","outcome":"refused","temperament":"fearful","lines":["No. I'll lose my post. No.","Please. I can't. Not me."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"fearful","lines":["All right! Anything. Stop looking at me.","Yes, yes. Only don't tell anyone."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["I drive the Councillor. Nothing else. Noted.","Move along, friend. This goes in my log."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pay","speaker":"driver","outcome":"refused","temperament":"idealist","lines":["I can't be bought. Not even by you.","Keep your money. Find someone cheaper."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pay","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"idealist","lines":["A bribe? I'll tell the Office.","Put it away, or I report you."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pay","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["Deal. Where do I put the car?","Half now, half later.","Cash? Say no more."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pay","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"fearful","lines":["Put it away! Someone's watching! Yes, fine.","Okay. Just take it quietly."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pay","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["I report bribes. Even polite ones.","Keep that. This goes in my log."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"idealist","lines":["That's decent of you. The car is yours.","My wages, covered? Then I'm with you."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"kept","temperament":"idealist","lines":["Decent again. I'm in this with you.","You keep surprising me. Good."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"idealist","lines":["Don't help me. I'll have to report it.","Kindness from you? I don't trust it."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"not-yet","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["A first instalment. I'll wait for more.","Some cash. And the rest?"]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["Paid in full. The car's yours.","That settles it. Where do I park?"]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"kept","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["Another envelope? I'm your man.","You pay well. I remember that."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"not-yet","temperament":"fearful","lines":["Some of it. But what if I'm caught?","Thank you. It's not enough yet."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"fearful","lines":["I can cover it now. I'll do what you ask.","You've saved me. I'll do it."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"kept","temperament":"fearful","lines":["You look after me. Thank you.","I sleep better since you came."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"not-yet","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Generous. I need a moment to decide.","A little more, and I'm yours."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"loyal","lines":["The Office won't hear it from me.","You came through. So will I."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"kept","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Reliable of you. I'll note that.","A steady friend. I won't forget."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Help from strangers? I'll write it down.","Favours get reported. I'm sorry."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"idealist","lines":["You're no better than the city. Fine.","I hate this. I'll do it once."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"idealist","lines":["I'll see you reported for this.","Threats? The Office will hear of it."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["No need for that. Name the job.","Threats don't raise my price. Fine."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"driver","outcome":"turned","temperament":"fearful","lines":["Please, no! I'll drive wherever you say.","Don't hurt me. I'll do it."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"driver","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Threatening an official's driver? Reported.","Say that again for the officer."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"guard","outcome":"refused","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["Free favours don't pay my rent.","Talk to me with an envelope."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"ask","speaker":"guard","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["State your business or move along.","You're loitering at an Office door. Move."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pay","speaker":"guard","outcome":"turned","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["The envelope's heavy. I'm looking away.","I never saw you. A pleasure."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pay","speaker":"guard","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Bribing an officer. Name and address?","That's a report I owe the Office."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"guard","outcome":"not-yet","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["Useful. Not enough yet.","A start. Keep going."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"guard","outcome":"turned","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["You've got me. What do you want?","Square. Now what?"]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"guard","outcome":"kept","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["You're generous. I like that.","More? You spoil me."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"guard","outcome":"not-yet","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Kind. But I still serve the Office.","I'll think it over. Come back."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"guard","outcome":"turned","temperament":"loyal","lines":["The Office comes first. After you, though.","Fine. You've earned a favour."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"guard","outcome":"kept","temperament":"loyal","lines":["You've earned my respect, citizen.","A steady friend. I won't forget it."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"help","speaker":"guard","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["Unusual help. I'll note the time.","Favours to an officer? Noted."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"guard","outcome":"turned","temperament":"mercenary","lines":["All right. I know when I'm beaten.","No need. I can be sensible."]},
  {"event":"reply","verb":"pressure","speaker":"guard","outcome":"suspicious","temperament":"loyal","lines":["A threat to an officer. Reported.","You'll answer for that to the Office."]},

The model never adds a kind (unknown = reject); Sky accepts a proposed kind as a rules change. One need per person. A record may narrow its kind's approaches, never widen them. No two records of an area differ only in wording: each differs in size, holder or kind. Phase 1: sizes are all standard, holders unset, one record per kind per area.",
